analysis.one_liner: Raises required new-car fuel economy to a combined 35 mpg average by 2013 and adds safety and consumer-labeling rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in February 2002 with 7 Senate sponsors, was referred to the Commerce Committee and never received a vote before Congress adjourned.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require automakers to raise the average fuel economy of new cars and light trucks, reaching a combined average of at least 35 miles per gallon by model year 2013, with annual steps starting in 2005 [S2] [S3]. It would create a system letting manufacturers buy and sell fuel-economy credits, require more accurate fuel-economy window stickers, add 'green label' and star ratings for efficient vehicles, allow hybrids and alternative-fuel vehicles to use carpool lanes, and direct the government to set stronger rollover and crash-protection safety standards [S2] [S3]. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and saw no further action [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Car buyers, who would save money at the gas pump as new vehicles become more efficient; taxpayers and drivers affected by reduced oil consumption and greenhouse gas emissions; and people in smaller cars, who would be better protected under the bill's new rollover and crashworthiness standards [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires average combined fuel economy of at least 35 mpg for cars and light trucks by model year 2013, with annual standards starting in 2005, including minimum levels of 33.2 mpg for cars and 26.3 mpg for light trucks by 2010 [S2] [S3].

Directs the Transportation Department to write new rollover crashworthiness standards (roof crush, seat and belt design, side-impact head airbags) and a standard to reduce damage to cars struck by light trucks by 30 percent [S3].

Requires fuel-economy testing to be revised so window-sticker numbers reflect real on-road performance within 5 percent by 2015, and requires trucks to carry the same fuel-cost and environmental labels cars do [S2] [S3].

Allows states to let solo drivers of hybrids and alternative-fuel vehicles use carpool lanes, and creates a 'green label' and star-rating program so shoppers can compare efficiency and emissions at the dealership [S2] [S3].
Sets a $5-per-0.1-mpg civil penalty floor for noncompliance, replacing the previous flat fine, so meeting the standards could not simply be treated as a cheap cost of doing business [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would bear the engineering cost of making cars and especially SUVs and pickup trucks dramatically more efficient, and to a lesser extent buyers of the least-efficient trucks, who would see those models phased toward higher mileage or higher prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance would impose real engineering costs on manufacturers, and some of that cost could show up in vehicle prices; the bill itself requires the Secretary to ensure progress on safety and U.S. employment, acknowledging that concern [S3].

The credit-trading system would let manufacturers that fall short buy their way to compliance from makers that exceed the standards, which could soften the real-world fuel savings if credit prices stay low [S3].

A sharp rise in standards on short timelines risks pushing consumers out of the large vehicles some households need, which is why the bill pairs the mandate with crash-protection standards and technology prize and cost-sharing programs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer and security benefits — lower fuel bills, less imported oil, fewer emissions, stronger rollover protection — were large relative to compliance costs that the auto industry ultimately absorbed in later decades when similar standards were adopted. The credit-trading mechanism and the flexibility it gives manufacturers are the main design weakness, but the bill pairs them with penalty floors and public reporting to limit gaming.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. John Kerry introduced the bill on February 8, 2002, for himself and Sen. Hollings, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1] [S5].
Six senators cosponsored the bill: five Democrats and one Independent [S4].
The committee took no further action — no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired with the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers, particularly those selling large SUVs and pickup trucks, avoided mandated fuel-economy increases and the associated engineering costs; consumers kept paying for inefficient vehicles at the pump.

for.name: John Kerry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise fuel-economy standards and add safety and labeling requirements.

for.name: Ernest Hollings
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Carolina, Chair of the Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's co-introducer in the Senate; his committee received the referral but never reported the bill.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 8, 2002 and took no further action; it never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split is unknown; all seven supporters were Democrats or Independents, and no senator is on record in opposition.

industries.industry: Automakers, especially light truck and SUV producers
industries.note: The bill would have required fleet averages of 33.2 mpg for cars and 26.3 mpg for light trucks by 2010 and 35 mpg combined by 2013, forcing major redesign of high-margin SUVs and pickups. Compliance costs would fall on manufacturers, while the savings — lower fuel bills, safer vehicles — would go to drivers.
Raising fuel economy across the new-vehicle fleet reduces gasoline demand over time, trimming a core revenue base. The bill's stated purposes include decreasing U.S. oil consumption as vehicle fuel.

The bill lets states open carpool lanes to solo drivers of hybrids and alternative-fuel vehicles and creates a $10 million-per-year prize competition for hybrid-electric light truck powertrains, creating demand and subsidies for efficient-technology makers.
